full_judgment:
9. Mr Tofailur Rahman, the learned Advocate appearing for the respondent Nos. 2 and 3, submits that no relief is available against the respondent Nos. 2 and 3 and Titas Gas Transmission and Distribution Company Limited itself being a statutory corporate body having not been impleaded as second party the petition is not competent and the relief as sought for could not be made effective even if it is granted by the Labour Court. He submits that Titas Gas Transmission and Distribution Company Limited had lost its autonomous character after it was taken over by the Government as abandoned property and placed under a Statutory Corporation namely, Bangladesh Minerals Oil and Gas Corporation pursuant to the Bangladesh Industrial Enterprises (Nationalisation) Order, 1972 (Presiden''s Order No. 27 of 1972). Mr Rahman submits that in view of the above position the order of the Labour Court cannot be implemented by the respondent Nos. 2 and 3 who were made second parties in the IRO Case b6fore the Labour Court. In support of his contention he made reliance upon a decision in the case of Musharraf Hossain Chowdhyry vs. General Manager, Titas Gas Transmission and Distribution Company Limited and others reported in 33 DLR (AD) 186. In that case the Appellate Division after examining the various provisions of President''s Order No. 16 of 1972 and also relevant provisions of President''s Order No. 27 of 1972 held that, "Titas Gas Transmission and Distribution Company lost its autonomous character after it was placed under the Minerals Oil and Gas Corporation after it was declared as an abandoned property. It was further observed that, with the nationalisation of the company and the consequent establishment of the corporation with control over its management and administration, whatever autonomous character it might claim to have previously, after it was declared as an abandoned property under President''s Order 16 of 1972 was bound to be negatived unless some contrary intention appears in the Nationalisation order namely, President''s Order 27 of 1972. Considering the various provisions of laws as contained in President''s Order No. 16 of 1972 and President''s Order No. 27 of 1972 under which the enterprise was first taken over by the Government as abandoned property and then nationalised and placed under the corporation and the enactment relating to the creation of the corporation, its powers and functions and the enactments which refer to and deal with public or nationalised enterpriese, it would be difficult to hold that the company or enterprise, namely, Titas Gas Transmission and Distribution Company Limited maintained the corporate character of a limited company after it was taken over by the Government as a nationalised enterprise and placed under the corporation. The Titas Gas Transmission and Distribution Company Limited is in fact controlled by the corporation. There is nothing in its Memorandum of Articles of Association to show that it maintained its autonomous character or separateness from the controlling hand of the corporation. It is noted here that by subsequent amendment namely, Bangladesh Oil Gas and Mineral Corporation (Amendment) Act (XI of 1989) the corporation may be called "Petrobangla". Titas Gas Transmission and Distribution Company is now one of the components of Petrobangla. 

 17. This court in the case of KM Faziul Haque vs. Chairman, Bangladesh Agricultural Development Corporation and others reported in 48 DLR (January Issue) page 27 following a decision of the Appellate Division in the case of Md Arfan Ali vs. Sonali Bank and others in Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 26 of 1992 observed that under section 3(2) of the BADC Ordinance the corporation shall sue and be sued by its own name BADC though a separate entity was not impleaded, some officers of the said corporation, like the Chairman, the General Manager and the Regional Manager were impleaded seeking reinstatement and in view of the above decision of the Appellate Division the petitioner should have impleaded BADC as a respondent being the necessary and proper party against whom relief is actually claimed. In that case an Officer of Bangladesh Agricultural Development Corporation was departmentally proceeded against and he was dismissed from service and after dismissal order he prayed for a copy of the inquiry report for the purpose of filing an appeal but the copy was not supplied and in the meantime, the matter was referred to the anti-corruption department and a case was started under section 409 of the Penal Code read with section 5(2) of Act II of 1947, and the said case was registered as Special Case No. 4 of 1982 and tried by the Divisional Special Judge and the incumbent was acquitted but the authority refused to reinstate him, then the said officers preferred a writ petition before this court, and from the side of the respondent it was contended that the writ petition is not maintainable as the petitioner has impleaded some officers of the corporation instead of impleading the corporation, the employer who can actually provide relief claimed by the petitioner and writ petition was held to be not maintainable on the ground that the BADC being a statutory body was not made respondent. The same principle is applicable here. In the instant case as we have already found that the enterprise namely, Titas Gas Transmission and Distribution Company which is a part of the statutory corporation was not made party, nor the Chairman of the corporation was impleaded as party and as a result Labour Court rightly held that for non-impleading the proper authority as second party the petition in IRO case is incompetent and not maintainable. The Labour Court in any view of the matter has not committed any error of law apparent on the face of the record.
